title: The TypeScript Type System
summary: TypeScript checks shape, not name — a value satisfies a type by having the right properties, whatever its declared type is called. Generics, unions, and inference all build on that one structural model.

slides.markdown:
TypeScript's type checker asks one question about every value: **does its shape match what's required?** Not "was it declared as this specific type," but "does it have the properties this type demands." That's **structural typing**, and it's the single idea that makes the rest of the type system click — why two unrelated interfaces can be interchangeable, why `interface` and `type` overlap so much, and why over-using `any` throws this whole mechanism away.

This topic builds structural typing first, then the practical vocabulary interviewers expect: `interface` vs `type`, unions and intersections, generics, and knowing when to let inference do the work versus annotating explicitly.

slides.subTitle: "Duck typing," checked at compile time
slides.markdown:
TypeScript is **structurally** typed: a value satisfies a type if it has the required shape, regardless of what type it was declared with, or whether it was declared with any named type at all.

```typescript
interface Point { x: number; y: number; }
function printPoint(p: Point) { console.log(p.x, p.y); }

const coords = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; // never declared as Point
printPoint(coords); // valid — coords has at least the shape Point requires
```

`coords` was never annotated as a `Point`, and has an extra `z` property besides — TypeScript doesn't care. It only checks that every property `Point` requires exists with a compatible type. This is the opposite of **nominal** typing (Java, C#), where a value must be explicitly declared as (or extend) the exact named type to be accepted, extra properties or not.

slides.subTitle: Where they differ, where they don't
slides.markdown:
For describing an object's shape, they're nearly interchangeable — the differences are narrow but real:

| | `interface` | `type` |
|---|---|---|
| **Object shapes** | yes | yes |
| **Unions/intersections directly** | no | yes — `type A = B \| C` |
| **Declaration merging** | yes — two `interface Foo {}` blocks combine | no — a duplicate `type Foo` is an error |
| **Extending** | `extends` | `&` intersection |

```typescript
interface User { name: string; }
interface User { age: number; } // merges — User now has both name and age

type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "error"; // a type alias can name a union directly
```

The practical rule most teams land on: `interface` for object/class shapes meant to be extended or merged (especially library-public APIs, where consumers might augment them), `type` for unions, tuples, and anything that isn't a plain object shape.

slides.sectionTitle: When to let inference work vs annotate
slides.markdown:
TypeScript infers types constantly, and fighting that with redundant annotations is noise, not safety:

```typescript
const count = 5;                 // inferred as number — annotating :number adds nothing
const items = ["a", "b"];        // inferred as string[]

function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; } // return type inferred too,
                                                                 // but often worth stating on public APIs
```

The practical guidance: let inference handle **local variables and internal implementation** — annotating `const count: number = 5` adds zero safety since the checker already knows. Annotate explicitly at **function boundaries meant to be a stable contract** — public API parameters and return types especially — so a function's signature documents intent and catches a mismatched implementation even before any caller exists. Annotating everything is cargo-culting; annotating nothing at a public boundary loses the documentation value type signatures provide.

slides.subTitle: Losing the point of TypeScript
slides.markdown:
`any` isn't "unknown type, checked carefully" — it's an explicit opt-out that disables checking for that value **and everything it touches downstream**:

```typescript
function process(data: any) {
  return data.user.profile.name.toUpperCase(); // compiles, no matter what `data` actually is
}
process({ wrongShape: true }); // runtime crash, zero compile-time warning
```

The insidious part isn't the parameter itself — it's that `any` is **contagious**: anything assigned from an `any` value becomes `any` too, silently, with no error at the point of contagion. A single `any` deep in a call chain can erase type safety for everything downstream of it, which is why a codebase can have decent-looking type coverage by file count while still crashing on obvious shape mismatches. The fix, when the type genuinely isn't known yet, is `unknown` (next topic) — it forces a check before use instead of skipping checking entirely.

slides.subTitle: Excess property checks are narrower than the rule suggests

slides.markdown:
A type annotation is a **compile-time claim**, checked against the code you wrote — it says nothing about data that enters your program from outside TypeScript's view: a `fetch` response, `JSON.parse`, user input, `localStorage`.

```typescript
interface User { id: number; name: string; }
const user = JSON.parse(rawString) as User; // "as" is a promise to the compiler, not a check
user.name.toUpperCase(); // compiles fine — and crashes at runtime if rawString didn't actually have `name`
```

`as User` is a **type assertion** — you're telling the compiler "trust me, this is a `User`," and it does, without generating any runtime check. If `rawString` is malformed, nothing catches it until `user.name.toUpperCase()` throws at runtime on `undefined`. This is the senior-level caveat every "TypeScript prevents bugs" claim needs: it prevents a category of bugs **within statically-checked code**, and does nothing at the boundary where untyped data enters — that boundary needs runtime validation (a schema library like Zod, or manual checks), not just an assertion.
